pedagogy.summary: Adding within 100 is taught as strategy work grounded in place value, not as an early column algorithm. Children partition, use known number bonds, and bridge tens: 46+7 becomes 46+4+3, 38+40 adds tens to tens leaving ones untouched. The concrete-pictorial-abstract progression (base-ten blocks, bead strings, number lines → jottings) makes the tens boundary visible before it is recorded symbolically.
bestPractices: Extend within-20 'make ten' bonds to numbers within 100 — 46+7 uses the same partition of 7 into 4+3 that 6+7 does (NCETM Spine 1.13: known within-ten facts applied to a two-digit + single-digit number)
Keep tens and ones distinct: for 38+40, add the multiple of ten to the tens and leave the ones alone, so the child feels tens land on tens
Use multiple connected representations for the same calculation — bead string, part-whole diagram, number line, and symbolic jotting — so the strategy transfers
Secure fluent partitioning of numbers to ten first; it is the explicit prerequisite for independent bridging
Ask the child to relate the mental strategy to a written record and justify it, not just state the answer (curriculum: explain the reasoning)
keyRepresentations: Bead string / 100-bead frame (bridging a ten made visible)
Number line with jumps (partition the added amount into a jump to the next ten, then the rest)
Hundred square (move along for ones, down for tens)
commonMisconceptions: Treating a multiple of ten as ones: 38+40 done as 38+4=42
Not bridging the ten: 46+7 done as 6+7=13, keeping the 3 and losing the extra ten (answer 43), or concatenating to 413
Adding the added amount to the wrong part (ones added to the tens digit)
Persisting with count-all/count-on-in-ones instead of using place value

learn.summary: Children aged 6-7 add within 100 using place-value strategies, not a column algorithm. They partition addends, use known number bonds to bridge a ten (46+7 as 46+4+3), and add tens to tens leaving the ones untouched (38+40=78). A concrete-pictorial-abstract progression (bead strings, base-ten blocks, number lines, then jottings) makes the tens boundary visible before it is recorded symbolically. The crossing-a-ten moment and the tens-onto-tens move are the two insights to build and check.

activities.title: Watch a ten compose when you cross the boundary
feedback: If the child computes the ones as 13 but writes only the 3 (answer 43) or strings digits as 413, return to make-ten within 20 on a bead string so the extra ten is seen composing, then carry that exact move up to 46+7. The crossed ten must not disappear.

If the child counts on in ones (54, 55, ... 62 for 53+9), do not ban the counting or penalise slowness: it is valid and matures as make-ten becomes automatic. Model the make-ten jump alongside their count so the efficient move becomes the natural one.
Praise relating the spoken strategy to the partition: 'you split 7 into 4 and 3 to land exactly on the ten'.
activities.rationale: Known within-ten facts and partitioning transfer to a two-digit-plus-single-digit sum; the make-ten bridging strategy depends on fluent partitioning of numbers to ten, and letting the child act on the boundary turns bridging into something observed rather than told. A live manipulative where loose ones visibly compose a ten (with a running count) makes the regroup concrete; this is one effective way to expose the structure, not the only possible one. Equivalent physical bead strings or base-ten blocks serve the same purpose.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils add and subtract using concrete objects, pictorial representations and mentally, including a two-digit number and ones, a two-digit number and tens, and two two-digit numbers; recall facts to 20 and derive related facts to 100.

Known within-ten facts and partitioning are applied to add a single-digit number to a two-digit number; the make-ten bridging strategy requires fluent partitioning of numbers to ten, and strategies are connected across multiple representations (tens frames, part-whole, number line, symbolic).
Unitising (treating one ten as a single entity) and exchange are the ideas children must grasp to calculate with numbers beyond ten; a digit's value depends on its position.
learnerActions: Start with 46 shown on a bead string or in a base-ten workspace
Add single ones one at a time, saying the running total aloud (47, 48, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53)

When the added one makes ten loose ones, see that they complete a ten (on a bead string, the next block of ten beads is filled; with base-ten blocks, swap the ten ones for a ten-rod), so the count goes 49, then 50, then on to 53
Re-tell what happened: 'I added 4 to reach 50, then 3 more to make 53', and link it to the partition 7 = 4 + 3
Repeat for 53 + 9 (bridge to 60 by adding 7, then +2)
activities.intendedInsight: Bridging a ten is not an arbitrary rule: the extra ten is physically composed from ten ones, and the make-ten partition (7 = 4 + 3) is the same move used within 20 applied at 46.

activities.title: Tens land on tens: add a multiple of ten
feedback: If the child gives 38 + 40 = 42 (adding 4 to the ones, saying 'four tens is a four'), rebuild with ten-rods: forty is four tens and joins the three tens already there. Confront the size mismatch — 42 is only just above 38, so it cannot be right after adding forty.
Reinforce order-independence: adding the 8 first or the 40 first both give 78.
activities.rationale: The curriculum expects adding a two-digit number and a multiple of ten; keeping tens and ones distinct prevents the common error of adding a multiple of ten as if it were ones. Base-ten rods make the place-value distinction tangible.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils add and subtract using concrete objects, pictorial representations and mentally, including a two-digit number and ones, a two-digit number and tens, and two two-digit numbers; recall facts to 20 and derive related facts to 100.
Unitising (treating one ten as a single entity) and exchange are the ideas children must grasp to calculate with numbers beyond ten; a digit's value depends on its position.
learnerActions: Start with 38 shown with three ten-rods and eight ones
Add four ten-rods, watching them join the tens while the eight ones stay untouched
State the total as 70 + 8 = 78, and say why the ones did not change
Check by a different order: add 30 + 40 = 70 first, then the 8 — confirm it gives the same 78
Contrast with the wrong move: 'is 38 + 40 the same as 38 + 4? why not?' — notice 42 is only 4 more than 38, far too small after adding forty
activities.intendedInsight: A multiple of ten joins the tens, not the ones; four tens combine with three tens to make seven tens, leaving the ones unchanged.

activities.title: Partition the addend with a part-whole picture
feedback: If the child splits 7 into something that does not reach 50 (e.g. 2 and 5), ask which part gets them exactly to the next ten from 46.
A labelled picture shows the structure but does not let the child perform the regroup themselves; pair it with hands-on bridging (first activity) so the felt move and the structure connect.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal or labelled part-whole diagram makes the partition and the ten-crossing explicit. It teaches the structure of the strategy; because the learner does not act on the boundary, it works best alongside, not instead of, hands-on regrouping.
sourceClaims: Known within-ten facts and partitioning are applied to add a single-digit number to a two-digit number; the make-ten bridging strategy requires fluent partitioning of numbers to ten, and strategies are connected across multiple representations (tens frames, part-whole, number line, symbolic).
learnerActions: Look at 46 + 7 with 7 shown in a part-whole model
Split the 7 into 4 (the amount needed to reach the next ten) and 3 (the rest)
Mark where the calculation crosses a ten (at 50) and label it 'this is where we cross a ten'
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing the partition that lands exactly on the next ten is what makes bridging efficient; the structure of the strategy can be seen even before acting it out.

activities.title: Connect the strategy to a written record and explain it
feedback: Efficient work: 46+7 by partitioning 7 into 4+3 (46+4=50, then +3=53); 38+40 by adding tens (30+40=70, then +8=78) leaving the ones untouched; 53+9 by bridging (53+7=60, then +2=62) or 53+10-1.
If the child only states answers, ask them to link the jotting to the number line and say why each step works.
activities.rationale: The curriculum asks pupils to relate the strategy to a written method and explain their reasoning; using multiple connected representations for the same calculation helps the strategy transfer. Consolidation items (fill-the-blank partitions such as 46 + ? = 50, 50 + ? = 53, and choosing the correct partition of 38+40 rather than the common 42 error) check retention after the insight is built.
sourceClaims: Known within-ten facts and partitioning are applied to add a single-digit number to a two-digit number; the make-ten bridging strategy requires fluent partitioning of numbers to ten, and strategies are connected across multiple representations (tens frames, part-whole, number line, symbolic).
learnerActions: For each of 46+7, 38+40, 53+9, carry out the mental strategy and write a matching jotting (e.g. 46 + 4 = 50, 50 + 3 = 53)
Show the same calculation as a number-line jump (a jump to the next ten, then the rest)
Explain aloud why the method works, not just the answer
Answer probes: 'Show on the number line why 46 + 7 lands on 53'; 'For 38+40, would adding the 8 first give the same answer? How do you know?'; 'What changes if it were 46 + 40 instead of 46 + 4?'
activities.intendedInsight: The mental strategy, the number-line jump, and the written jotting are the same story told three ways; being able to justify the reasoning is part of the objective.

constraints: Teach as strategy work grounded in place value, not as an early column algorithm.
Secure fluent partitioning of numbers to ten first; it is the explicit prerequisite for independent bridging.

Fill-the-blank and multiple-choice items rehearse, check and consolidate the strategy and suit practice after the insight is built; they do not let the child enact the ten-crossing regroup by hand, so pair them with the hands-on activity (and the part-whole scaffold) rather than using them to first build the strategy.
A labelled or tap-to-reveal part-whole picture shows the structure but does not let the child perform the regroup; it is a scaffold to pair with hands-on bridging, not a replacement.
Do not ban counting-on in ones or penalise slowness; it is a valid developmental strategy that matures as make-ten becomes automatic. Model the efficient jump alongside the child's count.

Optional interactive supports (dragging ones that compose a ten at the boundary, a running count, sliding ten-rods onto the tens, a toggle mirroring the action as a number-line jump and jotting) make the mechanism concrete but are examples, not required mechanisms; equivalent physical bead strings and base-ten blocks serve the same purpose.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources have NOT been re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The NCETM Spine 1 source (Segments 1.11 & 1.13) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claim with corresponding caution.

The source row rated a third spatial dimension and in-role dialogue as poor fits with reasoning that extra dimensions 'add nothing' and 'talk is not the bottleneck'. These are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and are not asserted here. Addition within 100 is a quantity-and-place-value idea that does not require a third spatial dimension, and spoken explanation remains valuable for the 'explain your reasoning' objective.

Arithmetic self-check performed: 46+7=53, 38+40=78, 53+9=62, 30+40=70, 70+8=78, 53+7=60, 60+2=62 all correct. The error patterns 42 (for 38+40) and 43/413 (for 46+7) are named only as misconceptions to diagnose and correct, never as valid answers.

The 'explain your reasoning' objective is drawn from the broader DfE curriculum; the specific quoted DfE claim does not state it, so its support rests mainly on the multiple-representations claim rather than a direct quotation.
The prerequisite reteach IDs in the original assessment (e.g. mt_THl9GLxwoL, mt_m1W6nTQJ2b) are internal identifiers and have been omitted from learner-facing guidance.

probeDeeper: Show me on this bead string (or number line) why 46 + 7 lands on 53.
You added the 40 first for 38+40 — would you get the same answer if you added the 8 first? How do you know?
Which of these three was easiest for you, and what was it about the numbers that made it easy?
What if it were 46 + 70 instead of 46 + 7 — what changes about how you'd do it?
assess.correctAnswer: 53, 78, 62. Efficient work: 46+7 by partitioning 7 into 4+3 (46+4=50, then +3=53) or make-ten; 38+40 by adding the tens (30+40=70, +8=78) leaving the ones untouched; 53+9 by bridging (53+7=60, +2=62) or 53+10−1.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats a multiple of ten as ones — 'thirty-eight plus forty is forty-two' (adds the 4, not 40)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild with ten-rods: forty is four tens, and it joins the three tens already there. Confront the size mismatch — 42 is barely more than 38.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 38+40 the child adds 4 to the ones rather than 40 to the tens, giving 42; explains 'four tens is a four'

errorPatterns.pattern: Doesn't bridge the ten — '46 plus 7: six and seven is thirteen, so forty-three' (keeps the 3, loses the extra ten) or concatenates to 413
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to make-ten within 20 on a bead string so the extra ten is seen composing, then carry that exact move up to 46+7.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 46+7 the child computes the ones as 13 but writes only the 3, or strings digits together; the crossed ten disappears

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts on in ones by finger or tally rather than using place value — accurate but slow, and fragile when the count is long
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT ban the counting or penalise the slowness — it is a valid strategy that matures as make-ten becomes automatic. Model the make-ten jump alongside their count so the two line up and the efficient move becomes the natural one.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 53+9 the child counts 54,55,…62 one by one instead of jumping to 60 then +2

responseLevels.gap: Combines digits without regard to place value (38+40→42) or gives 46+7 as 43/413; cannot reliably cross a ten.
responseLevels.full: Uses place-value partitioning or make-ten fluently on all three, keeps tens and ones distinct, bridges the ten correctly, and can relate the jotting to a number-line or written record and say why it works.
responseLevels.partial: Reaches answers by counting on in ones, or handles 38+40 but stumbles whenever a ten must be bridged; the method works on some items but not dependably across the boundary.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put these three in front of the child one at a time and ask them to work each out, thinking aloud and jotting if they wish: 46 + 7, then 38 + 40, then 53 + 9. Watch closely what happens on the two that cross a ten.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The two items that cross a ten (46+7, 53+9) separate a child who bridges using place value from one who mishandles the boundary and drops or concatenates the extra ten; 38+40 separates a child who adds tens to tens from one who adds the '4' of forty to the ones. A child using place value gets all three cleanly; a child guessing digit-by-digit fails predictably at the boundary.
